chapters.title: Chapter 1 — Imitation as the principle common to the arts
paragraphs: I propose to treat poetry in itself and its various kinds, noting the essential quality of each. I will inquire into the structure of plot necessary for a good poem; into the number and nature of the parts that compose a poem; and similarly into anything else that falls within the same inquiry. Following the natural order, let us begin with the principles that come first.

Epic poetry and Tragedy, Comedy and Dithyrambic poetry, and the music of the flute and lyre in most of their forms — all are, in their general conception, modes of imitation. They differ from one another in three respects: the medium, the objects, and the manner of imitation are distinct in each case.

Just as some people, by conscious art or mere habit, imitate and represent various objects through color and form, or through the voice; so in the arts mentioned above, the imitation is produced by rhythm, language, or 'harmony' — either singly or in combination.

Thus in flute and lyre music, only 'harmony' and rhythm are used; the same applies to other arts like the shepherd's pipe. In dancing, rhythm alone is used without 'harmony' — for even dancing imitates character, emotion, and action through rhythmical movement.

There is another art that imitates by means of language alone, either in prose or verse — and the verse may combine different meters or use only one. But this art has had no general name. There is no common term for the mimes of Sophron and Xenarchus and the Socratic dialogues on one hand, and for poetic imitations in iambic, elegiac, or similar meters on the other. People do add the word 'maker' or 'poet' to the name of the meter, calling some 'elegiac poets' or 'epic (hexameter) poets,' as if it were the meter and not the imitation that made the poet. Even when a treatise on medicine or natural science is written in verse, custom calls the author a poet — yet Homer and Empedocles have nothing in common but meter, so it would be right to call one a poet and the other a physicist. By the same principle, even if a writer combined all meters in his poetic imitation, as Chaeremon did in his Centaur (a medley of every kind of meter), we should still bring him under the general term 'poet.' So much for these distinctions.

There are also some arts that employ all the means mentioned above — rhythm, tune, and meter. Such are Dithyrambic and Nomic poetry, and also Tragedy and Comedy. The difference is that in the first two, all the means are combined throughout, while in the latter they are used now one, now another.
These, then, are the differences among the arts with respect to the medium of imitation.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — Objects of imitation
paragraphs: Since the objects of imitation are people in action, and these people must be of either a higher or lower type (for moral character mainly answers to these divisions, with goodness and badness as the marks of moral difference), it follows that we must represent people either as better than they are in real life, as worse, or as they actually are. The same is true in painting. Polygnotus depicted men as nobler than they are, Pauson as less noble, Dionysius as true to life.

It is evident that each of the modes of imitation just mentioned will exhibit these differences and become a distinct kind by imitating different objects. Such diversities can be found even in dancing, flute-playing, and lyre-playing. The same goes for language, whether prose or verse without music. Homer, for example, makes men better than they are; Cleophon as they are; Hegemon the Thasian (the inventor of parodies) and Nicochares (the author of the Deiliad) as worse than they are. The same holds for Dithyrambs and Nomes — different types may be portrayed, as Timotheus and Philoxenus differed in representing their Cyclopes. The same distinction marks off Tragedy from Comedy: Comedy aims at representing men as worse than they actually are, Tragedy as better.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — Manner of imitation
paragraphs: There is a third difference — the manner in which each of these objects may be imitated. With the same medium and the same objects, the poet may imitate either by narration (taking on another personality, as Homer does, or speaking in his own person), or by presenting all his characters as living and moving before us.

These, as we said at the start, are the three differences that distinguish artistic imitation: the medium, the objects, and the manner. So from one point of view, Sophocles is an imitator of the same kind as Homer — both imitate higher types of character. From another point of view, he is of the same kind as Aristophanes — both imitate persons in action. Hence, some say, the name 'drama' is given to such poems, since they represent action. For this reason the Dorians claim the invention of both Tragedy and Comedy. The claim to Comedy is made by the Megarians — both those of Greece proper, who say it began under their democracy, and those of Sicily, since the poet Epicharmus (much earlier than Chionides and Magnes) belonged there. Tragedy too is claimed by certain Dorians of the Peloponnese. In each case they appeal to language: their outlying villages they call kōmai, while the Athenians call them dēmoi; they argue that 'Comedians' got their name not from kōmazein ('to revel'), but from wandering kata kōmas, village by village, having been excluded contemptuously from the city. They add that the Dorian word for 'doing' is dran, while the Athenian is prattein.
This may suffice as to the number and nature of the various modes of imitation.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — Origin and development of poetry
paragraphs: Poetry seems to have sprung from two causes, each rooted deeply in our nature. First, the instinct of imitation is implanted in us from childhood — one difference between us and other animals being that we are the most imitative of living creatures, and through imitation we learn our first lessons. No less universal is the pleasure we feel in things imitated. Experience proves it: objects we view with pain in themselves, we delight to contemplate when reproduced with minute fidelity — such as the forms of the most ignoble animals or of dead bodies. The cause is that learning gives the liveliest pleasure, not only to philosophers but to people in general, though their capacity for learning is more limited. The reason people enjoy seeing a likeness is that in contemplating it they find themselves learning — inferring, perhaps, 'Ah, that is he.' If you happen not to have seen the original, the pleasure will not be due to the imitation as such, but to the execution, the coloring, or some such cause.

Imitation, then, is one instinct of our nature. The other is the instinct for 'harmony' and rhythm, meters being clearly sections of rhythm. Starting from these natural gifts, people gradually developed their special aptitudes until their rough improvisations gave birth to Poetry.

Poetry diverged in two directions, according to the character of the writers. Graver spirits imitated noble actions, the actions of good men. The more trivial sort imitated the actions of meaner people, at first composing satires while the others wrote hymns to the gods and praises of famous men. No author of satirical poetry can be cited earlier than Homer, though there were probably many. From Homer onwards examples can be cited — his own Margites, for instance, and other similar works. The appropriate meter was also introduced here; this is why the measure is still called the iambic or 'lampooning' measure, since it was the meter in which people lampooned one another. Thus the older poets were classified as either heroic or lampooning verse writers.

In the serious style, Homer is preeminent among poets — for he alone combined dramatic form with excellence of imitation. He also first laid down the main lines of Comedy by dramatizing the ludicrous instead of writing personal satire. His Margites stands to Comedy as the Iliad and Odyssey stand to Tragedy. But once Tragedy and Comedy emerged, the two classes of poets followed their natural bent: the lampooners became writers of Comedy, and the Epic poets were succeeded by Tragedians, since drama was a larger and higher form of art.

Whether Tragedy has yet perfected its proper types, and whether it is to be judged in itself or in relation to its audience, is another question. In any case, Tragedy — like Comedy — was at first mere improvisation. Tragedy originated with the authors of the Dithyramb; Comedy with those of the phallic songs (still in use in many cities). Tragedy advanced by slow degrees, each new element being developed in turn. After many changes it found its natural form, and there it stopped.

Aeschylus first introduced a second actor; he diminished the importance of the Chorus and assigned the leading part to dialogue. Sophocles raised the number of actors to three and added scene-painting. Only later was the short plot abandoned for one of greater scope, and the grotesque diction of the early satyric form for the stately manner of Tragedy. The iambic meter then replaced the trochaic tetrameter, which had originally been used when the poetry was satyric and had stronger affinities with dancing. Once dialogue had come in, Nature herself discovered the appropriate measure: the iambic is the most colloquial of all measures — we see this in the fact that conversational speech runs into iambic lines more often than any other kind of verse, rarely into hexameters, and only when we drop our colloquial intonation. The additions to the number of 'episodes' or acts, and the other accessories tradition tells us about, must be taken as already described — discussing them in detail would be too large a task.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 — Comedy and epic compared with tragedy
paragraphs: Comedy, as we have said, is an imitation of characters of a lower type — not bad in the full sense of the word, since the Ludicrous is merely a subdivision of the ugly. It consists in some defect or ugliness that is not painful or destructive. The comic mask, for an obvious example, is ugly and distorted but does not imply pain.

The successive changes through which Tragedy passed, and the authors of those changes, are well known. Comedy has had no such recorded history because it was not at first treated seriously. It was late before the Archon granted a comic chorus to a poet; until then, the performers were volunteers. Comedy had already taken definite shape before comic poets, distinctively so called, are heard of. Who furnished it with masks, prologues, or extra actors — these and similar details remain unknown. As for the plot, it came originally from Sicily; among Athenian writers, Crates was the first to abandon the 'iambic' or lampooning form and to generalize his themes and plots.

Epic poetry agrees with Tragedy in being an imitation in verse of higher characters. They differ in that Epic poetry uses only one kind of meter and is narrative in form. They differ also in length: Tragedy tries, as far as possible, to confine itself to a single revolution of the sun, or only slightly to exceed this limit, while Epic action has no time limit. This is a second point of difference, though at first the same freedom was allowed in Tragedy as in Epic.

Of their constituent parts, some are common to both and some peculiar to Tragedy. So whoever knows what is good or bad in Tragedy also knows about Epic poetry: all the elements of an Epic poem are found in Tragedy, but not all the elements of Tragedy are found in the Epic.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 — Definition of tragedy and its parts
paragraphs: Of the poetry that imitates in hexameter verse, and of Comedy, we will speak later. Let us now discuss Tragedy, restating its formal definition based on what has already been said.

Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament, the several kinds being found in separate parts of the play; in the form of action, not narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation of these emotions. By 'language embellished' I mean language that includes rhythm, 'harmony,' and song. By 'the several kinds in separate parts,' I mean that some parts use verse alone while others use song as well.

Since tragic imitation requires people in action, it follows first that Spectacular equipment will be a part of Tragedy. Next, Song and Diction — for these are the medium of imitation. By 'Diction' I mean the metrical arrangement of the words; 'Song' is a term everyone understands.

Tragedy is the imitation of an action, and an action implies personal agents — who necessarily possess certain distinctive qualities of character and thought. It is by these that we qualify actions themselves; thought and character are the two natural causes from which actions spring, and on actions all success or failure depends. Hence the Plot is the imitation of the action — by 'plot' I mean the arrangement of the incidents. By 'Character' I mean what makes us ascribe certain qualities to the agents. 'Thought' is required wherever a statement is proved or a general truth enunciated. Every Tragedy, therefore, must have six parts that determine its quality: Plot, Character, Diction, Thought, Spectacle, Song. Two of these are the medium of imitation, one is the manner, and three are the objects of imitation. These complete the list. These elements have been used by virtually every poet — every play contains Spectacular elements as well as Character, Plot, Diction, Song, and Thought.

But most important of all is the structure of the incidents. Tragedy is an imitation not of people but of an action and of life — and life consists in action; its end is a kind of action, not a quality. Character determines men's qualities, but it is by their actions that they are happy or the opposite. So dramatic action is not undertaken to represent character: character comes in as subsidiary to the actions. Hence the incidents and the plot are the end of a tragedy — and the end is the chief thing of all. Without action there can be no tragedy; without character there can. The tragedies of most of our modern poets fail in their rendering of character, and of poets in general this is often true. The same holds in painting: the difference between Zeuxis and Polygnotus is that Polygnotus delineates character well, while Zeuxis's style has no ethical quality. Again, if you string together a set of speeches expressive of character, well finished in diction and thought, you will not produce the essential tragic effect nearly as well as a play that, however weak in those respects, has a plot and artistically constructed incidents. Besides, the most powerful elements of emotional interest in Tragedy — Reversal of the Situation (Peripeteia) and Recognition scenes — are parts of the plot. A further proof is that beginners in the art achieve finish of diction and precision of portraiture before they can construct the plot. The same is true of almost all the early poets.

The Plot, then, is the first principle and as it were the soul of a tragedy; Character holds second place. A similar truth holds in painting: the most beautiful colors, laid on confusedly, will not give as much pleasure as the chalk outline of a portrait. Tragedy is the imitation of an action, and of the agents mainly with a view to the action.

Third in order is Thought — the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent in given circumstances. In oratory this is the function of the political art and of rhetoric. The older poets make their characters speak the language of civic life; the poets of our own time make them speak the language of rhetoricians. Character is what reveals moral purpose, showing what kinds of things a person chooses or avoids. Speeches, therefore, that do not make this manifest, or in which the speaker chooses or avoids nothing, are not expressive of character. Thought, on the other hand, is found wherever something is proved or disproved, or a general maxim is stated.
Fourth among the elements is Diction — by which I mean, as already said, the expression of meaning in words; its essence is the same in verse and prose.
Of the remaining elements, Song holds the chief place among the embellishments.

Spectacle has an emotional attraction of its own, but of all the parts it is the least artistic and least connected with the art of poetry. The power of Tragedy is felt even apart from representation and actors. Besides, the production of spectacular effects depends more on the stage machinist than on the poet.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 — Plot: magnitude and unity
paragraphs: These principles being established, let us now discuss the proper structure of the Plot, since this is the first and most important thing in Tragedy.

By our definition, Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is complete, whole, and of a certain magnitude — for there can be a whole that lacks magnitude. A whole has a beginning, a middle, and an end. A beginning is what does not itself follow anything by causal necessity, but after which something naturally is or comes to be. An end is what naturally follows something else, either by necessity or as a rule, but has nothing following it. A middle is what follows something and is followed by something. A well-constructed plot, then, must neither begin nor end at random, but conform to these principles.

A beautiful object, whether a living organism or any whole composed of parts, must not only have an orderly arrangement of parts but also be of a certain magnitude — for beauty depends on magnitude and order. A very small organism cannot be beautiful, since the view of it is confused, taking only an almost imperceptible moment. Nor can one of vast size be beautiful — the eye cannot take it in at once, and the unity and sense of the whole is lost (imagine an animal a thousand miles long). As with living bodies, so with the plot: a certain length is necessary, and one that can be easily held in memory. The limit of length in relation to dramatic competition and stage performance is no part of artistic theory — if a hundred tragedies had to compete together, the performance would be regulated by water-clock, as we are told was once the case. The limit set by the nature of the drama itself is this: the greater the length, the more beautiful the piece will be by reason of its size, provided the whole remains clear. To put it roughly, the proper magnitude is one in which the sequence of events, by probability or necessity, allows a change from bad fortune to good or from good to bad.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 — Unity of plot
paragraphs: Unity of plot does not, as some think, consist in the unity of the hero. Infinitely various are the incidents in one man's life that cannot be reduced to unity; and many are the actions of one man that cannot be made into one action. This explains the error of all poets who have composed a Heracleid, a Theseid, or other such poems. They imagine that, since Heracles was one man, the story of Heracles must also be a unity. But Homer, surpassing all others here too — whether by art or natural genius — seems to have happily seen the truth. In composing the Odyssey he did not include all of Odysseus's adventures, like his wound on Parnassus or his feigned madness at the mustering of the host (incidents with no necessary or probable connection). He made the Odyssey, and likewise the Iliad, center around an action that in our sense of the word is one. As in the other imitative arts the imitation is one when the object imitated is one, so the plot — being an imitation of an action — must imitate one action, and that a whole, with the structural union of the parts such that if any one of them is displaced or removed, the whole will be disjointed and disturbed. A thing whose presence or absence makes no visible difference is not an organic part of the whole.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 — Poetry vs history
paragraphs: It is also evident from what has been said that the function of the poet is not to relate what has happened, but what may happen — what is possible according to the law of probability or necessity. The poet and the historian differ not by writing in verse or prose. The work of Herodotus could be put into verse, and it would still be a kind of history, with meter no less than without it. The true difference is that one relates what has happened, the other what may happen. Poetry, therefore, is more philosophical and a higher thing than history, since poetry tends to express the universal, history the particular. By 'the universal' I mean how a person of a certain type will speak or act on occasion, by the law of probability or necessity — and it is this universality at which poetry aims when it attaches names to its persons. The 'particular' is, for example, what Alcibiades did or suffered. In Comedy this is already apparent: the poet first constructs the plot on the lines of probability and then inserts characteristic names — unlike the lampooners, who write about particular individuals. But tragedians still keep to real names. The reason is that what is possible is credible: what has not happened we do not at once feel sure to be possible; what has happened is manifestly possible, since otherwise it would not have happened. Still, there are some tragedies in which only one or two well-known names appear, with the rest fictitious; and in others, none are well known, as in Agathon's Antheus, where incidents and names alike are fictitious — and yet the play gives no less pleasure. We must not, then, at all costs keep to the received legends that are the usual subjects of Tragedy. It would be absurd to attempt it — even subjects that are known are known only to a few, and yet give pleasure to all. Clearly, then, the poet or 'maker' should be the maker of plots rather than of verses, since he is a poet because he imitates, and what he imitates are actions. Even if he chances to take an historical subject, he is no less a poet — there is no reason why some events that have actually happened should not conform to the law of the probable and possible, and in virtue of that quality he is their poet or maker.

Of all plots and actions, the episodic are the worst. By 'episodic' I mean a plot in which the episodes or acts succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence. Bad poets compose such pieces by their own fault; good poets do so to please the actors — since they write show pieces for competition and stretch the plot beyond its capacity, often forced to break the natural continuity.

But Tragedy is an imitation not only of a complete action, but of events inspiring fear or pity. Such an effect is best produced when events come on us by surprise, and the effect is heightened when at the same time they follow as cause and effect. The tragic wonder will be greater than if they had happened of themselves or by accident — for even coincidences are most striking when they have an air of design. We may instance the statue of Mitys at Argos, which fell on his murderer while he was watching a festival, and killed him. Such events seem not to be due to mere chance. Plots constructed on these principles are necessarily the best.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 — Simple and complex plots
paragraphs: Plots are either Simple or Complex, since the actions of which they are imitations obviously show a similar distinction. An action which is one and continuous, in the sense defined above, I call Simple when the change of fortune takes place without Reversal of the Situation and without Recognition.

A Complex action is one in which the change is accompanied by Reversal, Recognition, or both. These should arise from the internal structure of the plot, so that what follows is the necessary or probable result of the preceding action. There is all the difference between an event that happens propter hoc (because of this) and one that happens merely post hoc (after this).

chapters.title: Chapter 11 — Reversal, recognition, and suffering
paragraphs: Reversal of the Situation is a change by which the action veers around to its opposite, subject always to our rule of probability or necessity. Thus in the Oedipus, the messenger comes to cheer Oedipus and free him from his alarms about his mother, but by revealing who he is, he produces the opposite effect. Again, in the Lynceus, Lynceus is being led away to his death and Danaus goes with him intending to slay him — but the outcome is that Danaus is killed and Lynceus saved. Recognition, as the name indicates, is a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hate between persons destined by the poet for good or bad fortune. The best form of recognition is one coincident with a Reversal of the Situation, as in the Oedipus. There are other forms too: even inanimate things of the most trivial kind may, in a sense, be objects of recognition; we may recognize or discover whether a person has done a thing or not. But the recognition most intimately connected with the plot and action is the recognition of persons. This recognition, combined with Reversal, will produce either pity or fear — and actions producing such effects are precisely what Tragedy, by our definition, represents. Moreover, it is on such situations that the issues of good or bad fortune will depend. Recognition, being between persons, may happen one-sidedly (one recognizes the other, who is already known) or on both sides. Thus Iphigenia is revealed to Orestes by sending the letter; but another act of recognition is required to make Orestes known to Iphigenia.

Two parts of the Plot, then — Reversal of the Situation and Recognition — turn on surprises. A third part is the Scene of Suffering. The Scene of Suffering is a destructive or painful action, such as death on the stage, bodily agony, wounds, and the like.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 — Quantitative parts of tragedy
paragraphs: [The parts of Tragedy that must be treated as elements of the whole have been already mentioned. We now come to the quantitative parts — the separate parts into which Tragedy is divided: Prologue, Episode, Exode, Choric song. The last is divided into Parode and Stasimon. These are common to all plays. Peculiar to some are the songs of actors from the stage and the Commoi.

The Prologue is the entire part of a tragedy that precedes the Parode of the Chorus. The Episode is the entire part between complete choric songs. The Exode is the entire part with no choric song after it. Of the Choric part, the Parode is the first undivided utterance of the Chorus; the Stasimon is a Choric ode without anapaests or trochaic tetrameters; the Commos is a joint lamentation of Chorus and actors. The parts of Tragedy that must be treated as elements of the whole have been already mentioned; the quantitative parts — the separate parts into which it is divided — are listed here.]

chapters.title: Chapter 13 — The tragic plot
paragraphs: Following from what has been said, we must now consider what the poet should aim at and what he should avoid in constructing his plots, and by what means the specific effect of Tragedy will be produced.

A perfect tragedy should, as we have seen, be arranged not on the simple but on the complex plan. It should imitate actions that excite pity and fear — the distinctive mark of tragic imitation. It plainly follows, first, that the change of fortune presented must not be that of a virtuous man brought from prosperity to adversity: this moves neither pity nor fear; it merely shocks. Nor that of a bad man passing from adversity to prosperity: nothing could be more alien to the spirit of Tragedy; it has no tragic quality at all; it neither satisfies the moral sense nor calls forth pity or fear. Nor again should the downfall of an utter villain be exhibited. Such a plot would, no doubt, satisfy the moral sense, but it would inspire neither pity nor fear: pity is aroused by undeserved misfortune, fear by the misfortune of someone like ourselves. Such an event would therefore be neither pitiful nor terrible. There remains, then, the character between these two extremes — a man not eminently good and just, whose misfortune is brought about not by vice or depravity, but by some error or frailty. He must be highly renowned and prosperous — a figure like Oedipus, Thyestes, or other illustrious men of such families.

A well-constructed plot should, then, be single in its issue, rather than double as some maintain. The change of fortune should be not from bad to good, but from good to bad. It should come about not as the result of vice but of some great error or frailty, in a character such as we have described, or a better one rather than a worse. The practice of the stage bears this out. At first the poets recounted whatever legend came their way; now, the best tragedies are founded on the story of a few houses — on the fortunes of Alcmaeon, Oedipus, Orestes, Meleager, Thyestes, Telephus, and others who have done or suffered something terrible. A tragedy, then, to be perfect according to the rules of art, should be of this construction. So those who censure Euripides for following this principle in his plays — many of which end unhappily — are mistaken. As we have said, this is the right ending. The best proof is that on the stage and in dramatic competition, such plays, well worked out, are the most tragic in effect; and Euripides, faulty though he may be in the general management of his subject, is felt to be the most tragic of poets.

In the second rank comes the kind of tragedy that some place first. Like the Odyssey, it has a double thread of plot and an opposite catastrophe for the good and the bad. It is accounted the best because of the weakness of audiences — the poet is guided by the wishes of his audience. The pleasure derived from this is not the true tragic pleasure; it is proper rather to Comedy, where those who in the play are deadliest enemies — like Orestes and Aegisthus — leave the stage as friends at the close, and no one slays or is slain.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 — Pity and fear from incidents
paragraphs: Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacular means; but they may also result from the inner structure of the piece, which is the better way and indicates a superior poet. The plot ought to be so constructed that, even without the aid of the eye, anyone who hears the tale told will thrill with horror and melt with pity at what takes place. This is the impression we should receive from hearing the story of the Oedipus. Producing this effect by mere spectacle is a less artistic method, dependent on extraneous aids. Those who employ spectacular means to create not the terrible but the monstrous are strangers to the purpose of Tragedy: we must not demand of Tragedy any and every kind of pleasure, but only the kind proper to it. Since the pleasure the poet should afford is the kind that comes from pity and fear through imitation, this quality must clearly be impressed on the incidents.
Let us then determine what are the circumstances that strike us as terrible or pitiful.

Actions capable of this effect must happen between persons who are friends, enemies, or indifferent to one another. If an enemy kills an enemy, there is nothing to excite pity in either the act or the intention — except so far as the suffering itself is pitiful. The same is true with indifferent persons. But when the tragic incident happens between people who are near or dear to one another — if, for example, a brother kills, or intends to kill, a brother; a son his father; a mother her son; a son his mother; or any such deed is done — these are the situations the poet should look for. He may not destroy the framework of the received legends — the fact, for instance, that Clytemnestra was slain by Orestes and Eriphyle by Alcmaeon — but he should show invention of his own and skillfully handle the traditional material. Let us explain more clearly what is meant by skillful handling.

The action may be done consciously and with knowledge of the persons, in the manner of the older poets — as Euripides has Medea slay her children. Or the deed of horror may be done in ignorance, with the tie of kinship or friendship discovered afterwards: Sophocles's Oedipus is an example. Here the incident is outside the drama proper, but cases occur where it falls within the action of the play — as in Astydamas's Alcmaeon, or in Telegonus in The Wounded Odysseus. Again, there is a third case: about to act with knowledge of the persons and then not to act. The fourth is when someone is about to do an irreparable deed through ignorance and makes the discovery before it is done. These are the only possible ways. The deed must either be done or not done, knowingly or unknowingly. But of all these ways, to be about to act with knowledge of the persons and then not to act is the worst — it is shocking without being tragic, since no disaster follows. It is therefore never, or very rarely, found in poetry. One instance is in the Antigone, where Haemon threatens to kill Creon. The next and better way is for the deed to be carried out. Better still, that it be carried out in ignorance, with the discovery made afterwards. Then there is nothing to shock us, and the discovery produces a startling effect. The last case is the best — as when in the Cresphontes Merope is about to slay her son but, recognizing him, spares his life; or in the Iphigenia, where the sister recognizes the brother just in time; or in the Helle, where the son recognizes the mother when on the point of giving her up. This, then, is why a few families only, as we have already noted, furnish the subjects of tragedy. It was not art but happy chance that led the poets in their search for subjects to find the tragic quality in their plots. They are compelled, therefore, to turn to the houses whose history contains such moving incidents.
Enough has now been said about the structure of the incidents and the right kind of plot.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 — Character in tragedy
paragraphs: In respect of Character there are four things to be aimed at. First, and most important, character must be good. Any speech or action that manifests moral purpose of any kind will be expressive of character; the character will be good if the purpose is good. This rule is relative to each class — even a woman may be good, and also a slave, though a woman may be said to be an inferior being and a slave quite worthless. The second thing to aim at is propriety. There is a type of manly valor; but valor in a woman, or unscrupulous cleverness, is inappropriate. Third, character must be true to life — a distinct thing from goodness and propriety as just described. The fourth point is consistency: even if the subject of imitation, who suggested the type, is inconsistent, he must be consistently inconsistent. As an example of motiveless degradation of character we have Menelaus in the Orestes; of character indecorous and inappropriate, the lament of Odysseus in the Scylla and the speech of Melanippe; of inconsistency, the Iphigenia at Aulis — for Iphigenia the suppliant in no way resembles her later self.

As in the structure of the plot, so too in the portraiture of character, the poet should always aim at the necessary or the probable. A person of a given character should speak or act in a given way by the rule either of necessity or of probability — just as an event should follow another by necessary or probable sequence. It is therefore evident that the unraveling of the plot, no less than the complication, must arise out of the plot itself; it must not be brought about by the deus ex machina, as in the Medea or in the Return of the Greeks in the Iliad. The deus ex machina should be employed only for events external to the drama — for antecedent or subsequent events that lie beyond the range of human knowledge and require to be reported or foretold; for to the gods we ascribe the power of seeing all things. Within the action there must be nothing irrational. If the irrational cannot be excluded, it should be outside the scope of the tragedy. Such is the irrational element in Sophocles's Oedipus.

Again, since Tragedy is an imitation of persons above the common level, the example of good portrait painters should be followed. They, while reproducing the distinctive form of the original, make a likeness that is true to life and yet more beautiful. So too the poet, in representing men who are irascible or indolent or have other defects, should preserve the type and yet ennoble it. In this way Achilles is portrayed by Agathon and Homer.

These, then, are rules the poet should observe. Nor should he neglect those appeals to the senses which, though not among the essentials, are the concomitants of poetry — for here too there is much room for error. But enough has been said of this in our published treatises.

chapters.title: Chapter 16 — Forms of recognition
paragraphs: What Recognition is has been already explained. We will now enumerate its kinds.

First, the least artistic form, most commonly used out of poverty of wit: recognition by signs. Some signs are congenital — like 'the spear which the earth-born race bear on their bodies,' or the stars introduced by Carcinus in his Thyestes. Others are acquired after birth: bodily marks like scars, or external tokens like necklaces, or the little ark in the Tyro by which the discovery is made. Even these admit of more or less skillful treatment. Thus in the recognition of Odysseus by his scar, the discovery is made one way by the nurse, another way by the swineherds. The use of tokens for the express purpose of proof — and indeed any formal proof, with or without tokens — is a less artistic mode of recognition. A better kind comes about by a turn of incident, as in the Bath Scene in the Odyssey.

Next come recognitions invented at will by the poet, and on that account lacking in art. For example, Orestes in the Iphigenia reveals the fact that he is Orestes. She makes herself known by the letter; but he, by speaking himself, says what the poet — not the plot — requires. This is therefore close to the fault mentioned above: Orestes might as well have brought tokens with him. Another similar instance is the 'voice of the shuttle' in Sophocles's Tereus.

The third kind depends on memory: when the sight of some object awakens a feeling. Examples are the Cyprians of Dicaeogenes, where the hero breaks into tears on seeing the picture; or the 'Lay of Alcinous,' where Odysseus, hearing the minstrel play the lyre, recalls the past and weeps — and hence the recognition.

The fourth kind is by reasoning. Thus in the Choephori: 'Someone resembling me has come; no one resembles me but Orestes; therefore Orestes has come.' Such too is the discovery made by Iphigenia in the play of Polyidus the Sophist: it was a natural reflection for Orestes to make, 'So I too must die at the altar like my sister.' So again in Theodectes's Tydeus, the father says, 'I came to find my son, and I lose my own life.' So too in the Phineidae: the women, on seeing the place, inferred their fate — 'Here we are doomed to die, for here we were cast forth.' There is also a composite kind of recognition involving false inference on the part of one of the characters, as in Odysseus Disguised as a Messenger. A said that no one else could bend the bow; hence B (the disguised Odysseus) imagined that A would recognize the bow — which in fact he had not seen. The expectation that A would recognize the bow is a false inference.

But of all recognitions, the best is that which arises from the incidents themselves, where the startling discovery is made by natural means. Such is the recognition in Sophocles's Oedipus and in the Iphigenia — for it was natural that Iphigenia should wish to send a letter. These recognitions alone dispense with the artificial aid of tokens or amulets. Next come the recognitions by reasoning.

chapters.title: Chapter 17 — Practical advice for the poet
paragraphs: In constructing the plot and working it out with the proper diction, the poet should place the scene as far as possible before his eyes. Seeing everything with the utmost vividness, as if he were a spectator of the action, he will discover what is in keeping with it and be most unlikely to overlook inconsistencies. The need of such a rule is shown by the fault found in Carcinus: Amphiaraus was on his way from the temple, a fact that escaped the observation of someone who did not see the situation. On the stage, however, the piece failed, the audience being offended at the oversight.

The poet should also work out his play, to the best of his power, with appropriate gestures — those who feel emotion are most convincing through natural sympathy with the characters they represent: one who is agitated storms, one who is angry rages, with the most lifelike reality. Hence poetry implies either a happy gift of nature or a strain of madness. In the one case, a man can take the mold of any character; in the other, he is lifted out of his proper self.

As for the story, whether the poet takes it ready-made or constructs it for himself, he should first sketch its general outline, and then fill in the episodes and amplify in detail. The general plan can be illustrated by the Iphigenia. A young girl is sacrificed; she disappears mysteriously from the eyes of those who sacrificed her; she is transported to another country, where the custom is to offer up all strangers to the goddess. To this office she is appointed. Some time later her own brother chances to arrive. The fact that the oracle for some reason ordered him to go there is outside the general plan of the play. The purpose of his coming is also outside the action proper. However, he comes; he is seized; and when on the point of being sacrificed, he reveals who he is. The mode of recognition may be either Euripides's or Polyidus's, in whose play the brother very naturally exclaims, 'So it was not my sister only, but I too, who was doomed to be sacrificed' — and by that remark he is saved.

After this, the names being once given, what remains is to fill in the episodes. They must be relevant to the action. In the case of Orestes, for example, there is the madness which led to his capture, and his deliverance by means of the purificatory rite. In drama the episodes are short, but it is these that give extension to Epic poetry. Thus the story of the Odyssey can be stated briefly: a certain man is absent from home for many years; he is jealously watched by Poseidon and left desolate. Meanwhile his home is in a wretched plight — suitors are wasting his substance and plotting against his son. At last, tempest-tossed, he himself arrives; he makes himself known to certain persons; he attacks the suitors with his own hand and is preserved while he destroys them. This is the essence of the plot; the rest is episode.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 — Complication and unraveling
paragraphs: Every tragedy falls into two parts — Complication and Unraveling (Denouement). Incidents extraneous to the action are frequently combined with a portion of the action proper to form the Complication; the rest is the Unraveling. By Complication I mean all that extends from the beginning of the action to the part marking the turning point to good or bad fortune. The Unraveling extends from the beginning of the change to the end. Thus, in Theodectes's Lynceus, the Complication consists of the incidents presupposed in the drama, the seizure of the child, and so on; the Unraveling extends from the accusation of murder to the end.

There are four kinds of Tragedy: the Complex, depending entirely on Reversal of the Situation and Recognition; the Pathetic (where the motive is passion), such as the tragedies on Ajax and Ixion; the Ethical (where the motives are ethical), such as the Phthiotides and the Peleus. The fourth kind is the Simple — here we exclude the purely spectacular element — exemplified by the Phorcides, the Prometheus, and scenes set in Hades. The poet should try, if possible, to combine all poetic elements; or failing that, the greatest number and the most important — the more so, given the cavilling criticism of the day. Where there have hitherto been good poets each in their own branch, critics now expect one man to surpass all others in their several lines of excellence.

In speaking of a tragedy as the same or different, the best test is the plot. Identity exists where the Complication and Unraveling are the same. Many poets tie the knot well but unravel it badly. Both arts, however, should be mastered.

The poet should remember what has often been said and not make an Epic structure into a Tragedy. By an Epic structure I mean one with a multiplicity of plots — as if, for instance, you were to make a tragedy out of the entire story of the Iliad. In an Epic poem, owing to its length, each part assumes its proper magnitude. In drama the result is far from answering to the poet's expectation. The proof is that the poets who have dramatized the whole story of the Fall of Troy, instead of selecting portions like Euripides, or who have taken the whole tale of Niobe and not a part of her story like Aeschylus, either fail utterly or meet with poor success on the stage. Even Agathon has been known to fail from this one defect. In his Reversals of the Situation, however, he shows marvellous skill in striving for the popular taste — to produce a tragic effect that satisfies the moral sense. This effect is produced when the clever rogue, like Sisyphus, is outwitted, or the brave villain defeated. Such an event is probable in Agathon's sense of the word: 'It is probable,' he says, 'that many things should happen contrary to probability.'

The Chorus too should be regarded as one of the actors. It should be an integral part of the whole, sharing in the action — in the manner of Sophocles, not Euripides. In the later poets, the choral songs pertain as little to the subject of the piece as to that of any other tragedy. They are therefore sung as mere interludes, a practice first begun by Agathon. Yet what difference is there between introducing such choral interludes and transferring a speech, or even a whole act, from one play to another?

chapters.title: Chapter 19 — Thought and diction
paragraphs: It remains to speak of Diction and Thought, the other parts of Tragedy having been already discussed. As for Thought, we may assume what is said in the Rhetoric, to which inquiry the subject more strictly belongs. Under Thought is included every effect that has to be produced by speech, the subdivisions being: proof and refutation; the excitation of feelings such as pity, fear, anger, and the like; and the suggestion of importance or its opposite. It is evident that the dramatic incidents must be treated from the same points of view as the dramatic speeches when the object is to evoke the sense of pity, fear, importance, or probability. The only difference is that the incidents should speak for themselves without verbal exposition, while the effects aimed at in speech should be produced by the speaker as a result of the speech. What would be the business of a speaker if Thought were revealed quite apart from what he says?

As for Diction: one branch of the inquiry treats of the Modes of Utterance, but this province belongs to the art of Delivery and to the masters of that science. It includes such questions as: what is a command, a prayer, a statement, a threat, a question, an answer, and so forth. To know or not to know these things involves no serious censure on the poet's art. Who can admit the fault Protagoras imputed to Homer — that in 'Sing, goddess, of the wrath,' he gives a command under the idea that he utters a prayer? For to tell someone to do a thing or not to do it is, Protagoras says, a command. We may therefore pass over this as an inquiry that belongs to another art, not to poetry.

chapters.title: Chapter 20 — Parts of language
paragraphs: [Language in general includes the following parts: Letter, Syllable, Connecting word, Noun, Verb, Inflexion or Case, Sentence or Phrase.

A Letter is an indivisible sound — yet not every such sound, but only one which can form part of a group of sounds. Even animals utter indivisible sounds, none of which I call a letter. The sound I mean may be either a vowel, a semivowel, or a mute. A vowel is one which, without impact of tongue or lip, has an audible sound. A semivowel has such impact and an audible sound, like S and R. A mute has impact but by itself no sound, becoming audible only when joined to a vowel — like G and D. These are distinguished according to the form assumed by the mouth and the place where they are produced: aspirated or smooth, long or short, acute, grave, or intermediate in tone — an inquiry that belongs in detail to writers on metre.
A Syllable is a non-significant sound composed of a mute and a vowel: GR without A is a syllable, as also with A — GRA. The investigation of these differences belongs also to metrical science.

A Connecting word is a non-significant sound which neither causes nor hinders the union of many sounds into one significant sound; it may be placed at either end or in the middle of a sentence. Or, a non-significant sound that out of several significant sounds is capable of forming one significant sound — like amphi, peri, and the like. Or, a non-significant sound that marks the beginning, end, or division of a sentence — such, however, that it cannot correctly stand by itself at the beginning, like men, ētoi, de.

A Noun is a composite significant sound, not marking time, of which no part is in itself significant: in double or compound words we do not employ the separate parts as if each were significant. Thus in 'Theodorus' ('god-given'), the dōron ('gift') is not in itself significant.

A Verb is a composite significant sound marking time, in which, as in the noun, no part is in itself significant. 'Man' or 'white' does not express the idea of 'when'; but 'he walks' or 'he has walked' does connote time, present or past.

Inflexion belongs both to noun and verb. It expresses either the relation 'of,' 'to,' or the like; or that of number, whether one or many, as 'man' or 'men'; or the modes or tones of actual delivery, e.g. a question or command. 'Did he go?' and 'go!' are verbal inflexions of this kind.

A Sentence or Phrase is a composite significant sound, some at least of whose parts are in themselves significant. Not every such group of words consists of verbs and nouns — 'the definition of man,' for instance — and it may dispense even with the verb. Still, it will always have some significant part, like 'in walking' or 'Cleon son of Cleon.' A sentence or phrase may form a unity in two ways: by signifying one thing, or by consisting of several parts linked together. Thus the Iliad is one by the linking of parts; the definition of man is one by the unity of the thing signified.]

chapters.title: Chapter 21 — Kinds of words
paragraphs: Words are of two kinds: simple and double. By simple I mean those composed of non-significant elements, like gē. By double or compound, those composed either of a significant and non-significant element (though within the whole word no element is significant), or of elements that are both significant. A word may also be triple, quadruple, or multiple in form, like many Massilian expressions — for example, 'Hermo-caico-xanthus, who prayed to Father Zeus.'
Every word is either current, strange, metaphorical, ornamental, newly coined, lengthened, contracted, or altered.

By a current or proper word I mean one which is in general use among a people; by a strange word, one in use in another country. Plainly the same word may be at once strange and current, but not in relation to the same people. The word sigynon ('lance') is to the Cyprians a current term but to us a strange one.

Metaphor is the application of an alien name by transference: from genus to species, from species to genus, from species to species, or by analogy (proportion). From genus to species, as: 'There lies my ship' — for lying at anchor is a species of lying. From species to genus, as: 'Verily, ten thousand noble deeds hath Odysseus wrought' — for ten thousand is a species of large number, used here for a large number generally. From species to species, as: 'With blade of bronze drew away the life,' and 'Cleft the water with the vessel of unyielding bronze.' Here aryein ('to draw away') is used for tamein ('to cleave'), and tamein again for aryein — each being a species of taking away. Analogy or proportion is when the second term is to the first as the fourth to the third. We may then use the fourth for the second, or the second for the fourth. Sometimes we qualify the metaphor by adding the term to which the proper word is relative. Thus the cup is to Dionysus as the shield is to Ares. The cup may therefore be called 'the shield of Dionysus,' and the shield 'the cup of Ares.' Or again, as old age is to life, so is evening to day. Evening may therefore be called 'the old age of the day,' and old age 'the evening of life,' or, in Empedocles's phrase, 'life's setting sun.' For some terms of a proportion there is at times no word in existence; still the metaphor may be used. For instance, to scatter seed is called sowing; but the action of the sun in scattering his rays is nameless. Yet this process bears to the sun the same relation as sowing to the seed. Hence the poet's expression 'sowing the god-created light.' There is another way this kind of metaphor may be employed: we may apply an alien term and then deny one of its proper attributes — as if we were to call the shield not 'the cup of Ares' but 'the wineless cup.'
{An ornamental word...}

A newly coined word is one that has never been even in local use, but is adopted by the poet himself. Some such words there appear to be: ernyges ('sprouters') for kerata ('horns'), and aretēr ('supplicator') for hiereus ('priest').

A word is lengthened when its own vowel is exchanged for a longer one, or when a syllable is inserted. A word is contracted when some part of it is removed. Examples of lengthening: polēos for poleōs, and Pēlēiadeō for Pēleidou; of contraction: kri, dō, and ops, as in mia ginetai amphoterōn ops.
An altered word is one in which part of the ordinary form is left unchanged and part is recast — as in dexiteron kata mazon, where dexiteron is for dexion.

[Nouns in themselves are masculine, feminine, or neuter. Masculine: those ending in n, r, s, or in some letter compounded with s — these being two, ps and ks. Feminine: those ending in vowels that are always long, ē and ō, and — of vowels that admit of lengthening — those in a. Thus the number of letters in which masculine and feminine nouns end is the same, since ps and ks are equivalent to endings in s. No noun ends in a mute or a short vowel by nature. Three only end in i: meli, kommi, peperi; five end in y. Neuter nouns end in these two latter vowels, and also in n and s.]

chapters.title: Chapter 22 — Diction
paragraphs: The perfection of style is to be clear without being mean. The clearest style is one that uses only current or proper words; but at the same time it is mean — witness the poetry of Cleophon and Sthenelus. Diction is lofty and raised above the commonplace when it employs unusual words. By unusual I mean strange or rare words, metaphorical, lengthened — anything, in short, that differs from the normal idiom. Yet a style wholly composed of such words is either a riddle or jargon: a riddle if it consists of metaphors, jargon if it consists of strange or rare words. The essence of a riddle is to express true facts under impossible combinations. This cannot be done by any arrangement of ordinary words, but by metaphor it can. Such is the riddle: 'A man I saw who on another man had glued the bronze by aid of fire,' and others of the same kind. A diction made up of strange or rare terms is jargon. A certain infusion of these elements is therefore necessary to style; the strange or rare word, the metaphorical, the ornamental, and the other kinds mentioned will raise it above the commonplace and mean, while the use of proper words will keep it clear. Nothing contributes more to clarity of diction that is also remote from commonness than the lengthening, contraction, and alteration of words: by deviating in exceptional cases from the normal idiom, the language gains distinction; by partial conformity with usage, it gains clarity. Critics, then, are in error when they censure these licenses of speech and hold the author up to ridicule. Eucleides the elder declared it would be easy to be a poet if you might lengthen syllables at will. He caricatured the practice in the very form of his diction, as in the verse: 'Epicharēn eidon Marathōnade badizonta,' or 'ouk an g' eramenos ton ekeinou elleboron.' To employ such license obtrusively is grotesque; but in any mode of poetic diction there must be moderation. Even metaphors, strange or rare words, or any similar forms of speech, would have the same effect if used without propriety and with the express purpose of being ludicrous. How great a difference is made by the appropriate use of lengthening can be seen in Epic poetry by inserting ordinary forms in the verse. So again, if we take a strange or rare word, a metaphor, or any similar mode of expression, and replace it by the current or proper term, the truth of our observation will be manifest. For example: Aeschylus and Euripides each composed the same iambic line, but the alteration of a single word by Euripides — substituting the rarer term for the ordinary one — makes one verse appear beautiful and the other trivial. Aeschylus in his Philoctetes says: phagedaina d'ē mou sarkas esthiei podos.

Euripides substitutes thoinatai ('feasts on') for esthiei ('feeds on'). Again, in the line nyn de m' eōn oligos te kai outidanos kai aeikēs, the difference will be felt if we substitute the common words: nyn de m' eōn mikros te kai asthenikos kai aeidēs. Or, if for the line diphron aeikelion katatheis oligēn te trapesan, we read diphron mochthēron katatheis mikran te trapesan.
Or, for ēïones boōōsin, ēïones krazousin.

Again, Ariphrades ridiculed the tragedians for using phrases no one would employ in ordinary speech: dōmatōn apo instead of apo dōmatōn, retheōn, egō de nin, Achilleōs peri instead of peri Achilleōs, and the like. It is precisely because such phrases are not part of the current idiom that they give distinction to the style. He failed to see this.

It is a great matter to observe propriety in these several modes of expression — also in compound words, strange or rare words, and so on. But the greatest thing by far is to have a command of metaphor. This alone cannot be imparted by another; it is the mark of genius — for to make good metaphors implies an eye for resemblances.

Of the various kinds of words, the compound are best adapted to Dithyrambs, rare words to heroic poetry, metaphors to iambic. In heroic poetry all these varieties are serviceable. But in iambic verse, which reproduces, as far as may be, familiar speech, the most appropriate words are those found even in prose: the current or proper, the metaphorical, the ornamental.
Concerning Tragedy and imitation by means of action, this may suffice.

chapters.title: Chapter 23 — Epic structure
paragraphs: As to that poetic imitation which is narrative in form and uses a single meter, the plot ought, as in tragedy, to be constructed on dramatic principles. It should have for its subject a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end. It will then resemble a living organism in all its unity and produce the pleasure proper to it. It will differ in structure from historical compositions, which by necessity present not a single action but a single period — and all that happened within that period to one person or to many, however little connected. Just as the sea-fight at Salamis and the battle with the Carthaginians in Sicily took place at the same time but did not tend to any one result, so in the sequence of events one thing sometimes follows another and yet no single result is thereby produced. Such, indeed, is the practice of most poets. Here again the transcendent excellence of Homer is manifest. He never attempts to make the whole war of Troy the subject of his poem, though that war had a beginning and an end. It would have been too vast a theme, not easily embraced in a single view. Or if he had kept it within moderate limits, it must have been over-complicated by the variety of incidents. As it is, he detaches a single portion and admits as episodes many events from the general story of the war — such as the Catalogue of the Ships and others — thus diversifying the poem. Other poets take a single hero, a single period, or an action that is single but with a multiplicity of parts. So did the authors of the Cypria and the Little Iliad. For this reason the Iliad and Odyssey each furnish the subject of one tragedy, or at most two; while the Cypria supplies materials for many, and the Little Iliad for eight — the Award of the Arms, the Philoctetes, the Neoptolemus, the Eurypylus, the Mendicant Odysseus, the Laconian Women, the Fall of Ilium, and the Departure of the Fleet.

chapters.title: Chapter 24 — Epic compared with tragedy
paragraphs: Epic poetry must have as many kinds as Tragedy: it must be simple, complex, ethical, or pathetic. The parts also, with the exception of song and spectacle, are the same — for it requires Reversals of the Situation, Recognitions, and Scenes of Suffering. Moreover, the thoughts and the diction must be artistic. In all these respects Homer is our earliest and sufficient model. Each of his poems has a twofold character: the Iliad is at once simple and 'pathetic,' and the Odyssey is complex (for Recognition scenes run through it) and at the same time 'ethical.' Moreover, in diction and thought they are supreme.

Epic poetry differs from Tragedy in the scale on which it is constructed and in its meter. As regards scale or length, we have already laid down an adequate limit: the beginning and the end must be capable of being brought within a single view. This condition will be satisfied by poems on a smaller scale than the old epics, comparable in length to the group of tragedies presented at a single sitting.

Epic poetry has, however, a great special capacity for enlarging its dimensions, and we can see why. In Tragedy we cannot imitate several lines of action carried on at the same time; we must confine ourselves to the action on the stage and the part taken by the players. But in Epic, owing to the narrative form, many events transacted simultaneously can be presented; and these, if relevant to the subject, add mass and dignity to the poem. The Epic has here an advantage that conduces to grandeur of effect, to diverting the mind of the hearer, and to relieving the story with varying episodes. For sameness of incident soon produces satiety and makes tragedies fail on the stage.

As for the meter, the heroic measure has proved its fitness by the test of experience. If a narrative poem in any other meter, or in many meters, were now composed, it would seem incongruous. Of all measures the heroic is the stateliest and most massive — and so it most readily admits rare words and metaphors, another point where the narrative form of imitation stands alone. The iambic and the trochaic tetrameter are stirring measures, the latter akin to dancing, the former expressive of action. Still more absurd would it be to mix together different meters, as Chaeremon did. Hence no one has ever composed a poem on a great scale in any other than heroic verse. Nature herself, as we have said, teaches the choice of the proper measure.

Homer, admirable in all respects, has the special merit of being the only poet who rightly appreciates the part he should take himself. The poet should speak as little as possible in his own person, since it is not this that makes him an imitator. Other poets appear themselves on the scene throughout, and imitate but little and rarely. Homer, after a few prefatory words, at once brings in a man, woman, or other character, none of them lacking distinctive qualities — each with a character of his own.

The element of the wonderful is required in Tragedy. The irrational, on which the wonderful chiefly depends for its effects, has wider scope in Epic poetry, because there the person acting is not seen. The pursuit of Hector would be ludicrous if placed on the stage — the Greeks standing still and not joining in, with Achilles waving them back. But in Epic the absurdity passes unnoticed. The wonderful is pleasing — as we may infer from the fact that everyone tells a story with some addition of his own, knowing his hearers like it. It is Homer who has chiefly taught other poets the art of telling lies skillfully. The secret lies in a fallacy: assuming that if one thing is or becomes, a second is or becomes, men imagine that, if the second is, the first likewise is or becomes. But this is a false inference. Hence, where the first thing is untrue, it is quite unnecessary, provided the second be true, to add that the first is or has become. The mind, knowing the second to be true, falsely infers the truth of the first. There is an example of this in the Bath Scene of the Odyssey.

Accordingly, the poet should prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities. The tragic plot must not be composed of irrational parts. Everything irrational should, if possible, be excluded; or at all events it should lie outside the action of the play (as, in the Oedipus, the hero's ignorance about the manner of Laius's death) — not within the drama, as in the Electra (the messenger's account of the Pythian games), or in the Mysians (the man who has come from Tegea to Mysia and is still speechless). The plea that otherwise the plot would have been ruined is ridiculous: such a plot should not have been constructed in the first place. But once the irrational has been introduced and an air of likelihood imparted to it, we must accept it in spite of the absurdity. Even the irrational incidents in the Odyssey, where Odysseus is left on the shore of Ithaca, would have been intolerable if treated by an inferior poet. As it is, the absurdity is veiled by the poetic charm with which Homer invests it.

The diction should be elaborated in the pauses of the action, where there is no expression of character or thought. Conversely, character and thought are merely obscured by a diction that is over brilliant.

chapters.title: Chapter 25 — Critical objections answered
paragraphs: With respect to critical difficulties and their solutions, the number and nature of the sources from which they may be drawn may be set out as follows.

The poet, being an imitator like a painter or any other artist, must of necessity imitate one of three objects: things as they were or are; things as they are said or thought to be; or things as they ought to be. The vehicle of expression is language — current terms or, it may be, rare words or metaphors. There are also many modifications of language that we concede to poets. Add that the standard of correctness is not the same in poetry as in politics, any more than in poetry as in any other art. Within the art of poetry itself there are two kinds of faults: those that touch its essence and those that are accidental. If a poet has chosen to imitate something but has imitated it incorrectly through lack of capacity, the error is inherent in the poetry. But if the failure is due to a wrong choice — if, for instance, he has represented a horse as throwing out both off legs at once, or introduced technical inaccuracies in medicine or any other art — the error is not essential to the poetry. These are the points of view from which we should consider and answer the objections raised by critics.

First, as to matters concerning the poet's own art. If he describes the impossible, he is guilty of an error; but the error may be justified if the end of the art is thereby attained (the end being that already mentioned) — that is, if the effect of this or any other part of the poem is rendered more striking. A case in point is the pursuit of Hector. If, however, the end might have been as well or better attained without violating the special rules of the poetic art, the error is not justified — for every kind of error should, if possible, be avoided.
Again: does the error touch the essentials of the poetic art, or some accident of it? Not knowing that a hind has no horns is a less serious matter than to paint it inartistically.

If it be objected that the description is not true to fact, the poet may reply, 'But the objects are as they ought to be' — just as Sophocles said that he drew men as they ought to be, while Euripides drew them as they are. In this way the objection may be met. If, however, the representation is of neither kind, the poet may answer, 'This is how men say the thing is.' This applies to tales about the gods. It may well be that these stories are neither higher than fact nor true to fact: they are very possibly what Xenophanes says of them. But anyhow, 'this is what is said.' Again, a description may be no better than the fact: 'still, it was the fact' — as in the passage about the arms: 'Upright upon their butt-ends stood the spears.' This was the custom then, as it now is among the Illyrians.

In examining whether what has been said or done by someone is poetically right or not, we must not look merely at the particular act or saying and ask whether it is poetically good or bad. We must also consider by whom it is said or done, to whom, when, by what means, or for what end — whether, for instance, it is to secure a greater good or avert a greater evil.

Other difficulties may be resolved by due regard for the usage of language. We may note a rare word, as in ourēas men prōton, where the poet perhaps uses ourēas not in the sense of mules, but of sentinels. So again of Dolon: 'ill-favoured indeed he was to look upon.' It is not meant that his body was ill-shaped, but that his face was ugly — for the Cretans use the word eueides ('well-favoured') to denote a fair face. Again, zōroteron de keraie ('mix the drink livelier') does not mean 'mix it stronger' as for hard drinkers, but 'mix it quicker.'

Sometimes an expression is metaphorical, as 'Now all gods and men were sleeping through the night,' while at the same time the poet says: 'Often indeed as he turned his gaze to the Trojan plain, he marvelled at the sound of flutes and pipes.' 'All' is here used metaphorically for 'many,' all being a species of many. So in the verse, 'alone she hath no part...,' oiē ('alone') is metaphorical: the best known may be called the only one.
Again, the solution may depend on accent or breathing. Thus Hippias of Thasos solved the difficulties in the lines didomen (didomen) de hoi, and to men ou (ou) katapythetai ombrō.
Or the question may be solved by punctuation, as in Empedocles: 'Of a sudden things became mortal that before had learnt to be immortal, and things unmixed before mixed.'
Or by ambiguity of meaning — as parōchēken de pleō nyx, where pleō is ambiguous.

Or by the usage of language. Any mixed drink is called oinos ('wine'). Hence Ganymede is said 'to pour the wine to Zeus,' though the gods do not drink wine. So too workers in iron are called chalkeas ('workers in bronze'). This, however, may also be taken as a metaphor.

Again, when a word seems to involve some inconsistency of meaning, we should consider how many senses it may bear in the particular passage. For example, 'there was stayed the spear of bronze' — we should ask in how many ways we may take 'being checked there.' The true mode of interpretation is the precise opposite of what Glaucon mentions. Critics, he says, jump at certain groundless conclusions; they pass adverse judgment and then proceed to reason on it; and assuming the poet has said whatever they happen to think, they find fault if a thing is inconsistent with their fancy. The question about Icarius has been treated this way. Critics imagine he was a Lacedaemonian and think it strange, therefore, that Telemachus did not meet him on going to Lacedaemon. But the Cephallenian story may perhaps be the true one: they allege that Odysseus took a wife from among themselves, and that her father was Icadius, not Icarius. It is merely a mistake, then, that gives plausibility to the objection.

In general, the impossible must be justified by reference to artistic requirements, to the higher reality, or to received opinion. With respect to the requirements of art, a probable impossibility is to be preferred to an improbable possibility. It may be impossible that there should be men such as Zeuxis painted. 'Yes,' we say, 'but the impossible is the higher thing — for the ideal type must surpass the reality.' To justify the irrational, we appeal to what is commonly said to be. In addition we urge that the irrational sometimes does not violate reason — just as 'it is probable that a thing may happen contrary to probability.'

Things that sound contradictory should be examined by the same rules as in dialectical refutation: whether the same thing is meant, in the same relation, and in the same sense. We should therefore solve the question by reference to what the poet says himself, or to what is tacitly assumed by a person of intelligence.

The element of the irrational, and similarly depravity of character, are justly censured when there is no inner necessity for introducing them. Such is the irrational element in Euripides's introduction of Aegeus, and the badness of Menelaus in the Orestes.

Thus, there are five sources from which critical objections are drawn. Things are censured either as impossible, as irrational, as morally hurtful, as contradictory, or as contrary to artistic correctness. The answers should be sought under the twelve heads above mentioned.

chapters.title: Chapter 26 — Epic vs tragedy: which is higher?
paragraphs: The question may be raised whether Epic or Tragic mode of imitation is the higher. If the more refined art is the higher, and the more refined in every case is what appeals to the better sort of audience, the art that imitates anything and everything is manifestly the most unrefined. The audience is supposed too dull to comprehend unless something of their own is thrown in by the performers — who therefore indulge in restless movements. Bad flute-players twist and twirl if they have to represent 'the quoit-throw,' or hustle the coryphaeus when they perform the 'Scylla.' Tragedy, it is said, has this same defect. We may compare the opinion the older actors held of their successors. Mynniscus used to call Callippides 'ape' on account of the extravagance of his action, and the same view was held of Pindarus. Tragic art as a whole stands to Epic in the same relation as the younger to the elder actors. So we are told that Epic poetry is addressed to a cultivated audience who do not need gesture, while Tragedy is addressed to an inferior public. Being then unrefined, it is evidently the lower of the two.

First, this censure attaches not to the poetic but to the histrionic art — gesticulation may be equally overdone in epic recitation, as by Sosistratus, or in lyrical competition, as by Mnasitheus the Opuntian. Next, all action is not to be condemned, any more than all dancing — only that of bad performers. Such was the fault found in Callippides, as in others of our own day, censured for representing degraded women. Tragedy, like Epic poetry, produces its effect even without action — it reveals its power by mere reading. If, then, in all other respects it is superior, this fault is not inherent in it.

And superior it is, because it has all the epic elements (it may even use the epic meter) plus music and spectacular effects as important accessories — and these produce the most vivid pleasures. Further, it has vividness of impression in reading as well as in representation. Moreover, the art attains its end within narrower limits, since the concentrated effect is more pleasurable than one which is spread over a long time and so diluted. What, for example, would be the effect of Sophocles's Oedipus if it were cast into a form as long as the Iliad? Once more: Epic imitation has less unity, as is shown by the fact that any Epic poem will furnish subjects for several tragedies. Thus if the story adopted by the poet has a strict unity, it must either be concisely told and appear truncated, or, if it conforms to the Epic canon of length, it must seem weak and watery. Such length implies some loss of unity if, I mean, the poem is constructed out of several actions, like the Iliad and the Odyssey, which have many such parts, each with a certain magnitude of its own. Yet these poems are as perfect as possible in structure: each is, in the highest degree attainable, an imitation of a single action.

If, then, Tragedy is superior to Epic poetry in all these respects, and moreover fulfils its specific function better — for each art ought to produce, not any chance pleasure, but the pleasure proper to it, as already stated — it plainly follows that Tragedy is the higher art, attaining its end more perfectly.

This much may suffice concerning Tragic and Epic poetry in general — their several kinds and parts, with the number of each and their differences; the causes that make a poem good or bad; the objections of the critics and the answers to these objections.
